OCBC Beats Expectations While DBS and UOB Miss: What Happened in 3Q 2026?
article:
If you own shares in
Singapore’s local banks
, last week was a busy one.
United Overseas Bank Limited
(SGX: U11), or UOB, reported last Wednesday, 4 November 2026, followed by
DBS Group Holdings Ltd
(SGX: D05) on Thursday.
Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation Limited
(SGX: O39), or OCBC, wrapped things up on Friday morning.
Only OCBC delivered a profit above analysts’ estimates for the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026).
Before you read too much into that, remember that a “beat” or a “miss” only compares a bank’s results with a forecast.
It doesn’t tell you whether the business is getting stronger or weaker.
For that, you need to dig deeper.
OCBC: How did a bank with lower income beat forecasts?
OCBC’s net profit rose 3.2% year on year (YoY) to S$2.04 billion, just above the S$2.01 billion average estimate from four analysts polled by LSEG.
In other words, the beat was a narrow one, at about 1.5%.
Total income slipped 1.7% YoY to S$3.73 billion.
Insurance income fell 37% to S$198 million as
Great Eastern Holdings Limited
(SGX: G07) booked mark-to-market losses on its bond portfolio.
Look past the insurance arm, and you’ll find a bank in good shape.
OCBC’s banking operations posted a record net profit of S$1.90 billion, up 16% YoY.
Customer loans grew 14% in constant-currency terms to S$372 billion, which lifted net interest income (NII) by 3.9% to S$2.3 billion.
That’s despite a net interest margin (NIM) that narrowed to 1.66% from 1.84%.
Trading income dipped 10.2% to S$465 million, the mildest decline among the three banks.
If you’re waiting for a
dividend
, it’s not due yet.
OCBC pays dividends only at its half-year and full-year results.
Management has raised its 2026 guidance to low-double-digit loan growth and kept its 50% dividend payout ratio.
DBS: Why did a growing bank miss forecasts?
DBS’s net profit fell 4.8% YoY to S$2.81 billion, short of the S$2.90 billion LSEG consensus.
The main culprit was markets trading income, which fell 65% YoY to S$152 million amid unfavourable equity market conditions.
Set that aside, and the core business kept growing.
Customer loans rose 9.5% to S$478.6 billion.
NII climbed 3.7% to S$3.71 billion even though NIM narrowed to 1.87% from 1.96%.
Net fee and commission income grew 6% to S$1.43 billion.
If you own DBS, you have a dividend coming, as it is the only local bank that pays one every quarter.
The bank declared an ordinary dividend of S$0.66 per share, 10% higher than the S$0.60 paid a year ago.
On top of that, you’ll receive a capital return dividend of S$0.15 per share, unchanged from a year ago.
UOB: Why did profit more than double yet still miss?
UOB’s net profit rose 182.2% YoY to S$1.25 billion.
Don’t let that number fool you.
A year ago, UOB set aside S$1.36 billion in allowances, which shrank its 3Q2025 profit to S$443 million.
Against forecasts, UOB missed by the widest margin.
Profit came in about 7.4% below the S$1.35 billion LSEG estimate.
Trading and investment income fell 33% YoY to S$322 million.
UOB’s NIM also narrowed to 1.68%, down 6 basis points from the previous quarter as funding costs rose.
Management now expects full-year NIM below 1.75%, down from its earlier guidance of 1.75% to 1.80%.
On the flip side, UOB’s fee business hit a record.
Net fee income rose 19% to S$733 million, with wealth management fees reaching a record S$258 million.
The non-performing loan (NPL) ratio eased to 1.5% from 1.6%.
Like OCBC, UOB pays dividends twice a year, so no dividend was due this quarter.
What do the three results tell you?
Trading income fell at all three banks.
UOB also faced a shrinking margin.
Here’s the thing: the parts of each bank that fund your dividends kept growing.
All three banks grew their loans and NII YoY.
All three also lowered their NPL ratios.
Get Smart: Look past the scorecard
When a bank misses forecasts, it’s tempting to treat it as bad news.
But a forecast is a guess about a single quarter.
Your dividends depend on years of lending and fee income.
So the next time a bank misses, ask yourself one question: did the miss come from trading, or from the core business?
Trading income rises and falls with the markets.
A shrinking loan book or a rise in bad loans is a far bigger warning sign for your dividends.
This quarter, all three banks passed that test.
The number to keep an eye on next is NIM.
OCBC expects
higher US interest rates
to lift its NII as its assets reprice, while UOB has just cut its margin guidance.
How each bank handles interest rates in 2027 will shape how much your dividends can grow.

title: Mitsui Chemicals to take over chip linchpin JSR for US$12 bil
article:
(Nov 9): Japan’s Mitsui Chemicals Inc is buying JSR Corp for ¥1.84 trillion (US$12 billion) with support from state-backed Development Bank of Japan (DBJ) to strengthen its hold over a key chip materials linchpin.

Mitsui Chemicals and DBJ will acquire all shares of JSR from government-backed Japan Investment Corp, the companies said in a filing Monday. DBJ will pay ¥200 billion in cash for a stake that will be converted to preferred shares without voting rights, it said.

The deal for JSR, one of the world’s leading makers of photoresists needed to make advanced chips, would further a government-backed effort to consolidate Japan’s fragmented semiconductor-materials industry. Japan is home to the world’s largest suppliers of silicon wafers and dominates several other critical chip materials, but many of its smaller suppliers remain vulnerable to foreign takeovers.

Mitsui Chemicals’ shares extended their decline to as much as 15% in Tokyo.

JIC took JSR private two years ago. JSR supplies light-sensitive materials used with ASML Holding NV’s extreme ultraviolet lithography machines to pattern fine circuits onto silicon wafers. Customers for JSR’s array of specialty chemicals include Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, Intel Corp and Samsung Electronics Co, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

Bloomberg News reported in September that JSR was weighing buyout proposals from Mitsui Chemicals and rival Mitsubishi Chemical Group Corp.

title: Lula vows fiscal responsibility in first address since election
article:
(Nov 9): President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva pledged to preserve Brazil’s public finances without abandoning social programmes in his first televised address since winning a fourth term, as he sought to reassure investors.

“The trajectory of public debt and high interest rates concern me, which is why I reaffirm my commitment to fiscal responsibility, in order to make sustainable social policies possible and enable the much-needed expansion of investment,” Lula said in his Sunday remarks. “All of this will be done while preserving the fiscal rules.”

He cited lowering interest rates as one of the main challenges ahead, saying his government will create the conditions to reduce borrowing costs and help raise investment in the country to more than 20% of GDP.

The president, however, offered no details on spending cuts, revenue measures or other steps his administration could take to shore up the public accounts, a key concern for investors as he prepares for another four years in office.

The message marks an early attempt by the leftist leader to balance competing pressures: preserving the social agenda that has defined his political career while convincing investors his government can keep public finances under control and create conditions for interest rates to fall.

Brazilian assets have come under heavy pressure since Lula’s surprise runoff victory, amid market concerns that his fiscal approach will exacerbate budgetary strains and further complicate the central bank’s efforts to tamp down inflation.

See also: UBS CEO Ermotti says midterms create uncertainty for AI buildout

In his public address, Lula highlighted some of his government’s key achievements, including the passage of a shorter workweek. He also pledged to expand a series of government programs, including measures aimed at supporting small businesses.Lula, who was reelected on Oct. 25, used the roughly 8-minute address to thank Brazilians for giving him another term, with particular mention of young people, women and the elderly. He also sought to strike a conciliatory tone after a deeply divisive campaign, pledging to govern for all Brazilians and work to normalize political relations in the country.

“I am immensely grateful for the more than 64 million votes I received, and I will govern for all Brazilian women and men, as I have always done. We must build bridges instead of walls,” he said.

The 81-year-old leader, now entering his fourth term as Brazil’s president, faces a slowing economy and a growing number of families grappling with debt. In his speech, Lula highlighted a series of measures aimed at easing the financial burden on Brazilian households, including an income-tax exemption for those earning up to 5,000 reais (US$907) a month and a ban on online gambling.

See also: RBA’s Hunter says AI boom will put near-term pressure on CPI

“Without spending money on bets, families have increased consumption, retailers are selling more, industry is producing more and the wheels of the economy are turning again,” he said. “Betting destroyed lives and must remain in the past, like a nightmare from which Brazil has finally awakened.”

title: UBS CEO Ermotti says midterms create uncertainty for AI buildout
article:
(Nov 9): UBS Group AG chief executive officer Sergio Ermotti said the sweep of Democrats in the US midterm elections could trigger a slowdown in the construction of artificial intelligence capacity.

“Investors are rightly questioning the plausibility of how much value can be created out of this cycle,” he said in a Bloomberg Television interview in Sydney on Monday. “The problem being more on the timing, on how quickly can you really deliver all these benefits, and in that sense, you see a little bit of questioning around valuations that is important.”

Candidates who favor stricter oversight of AI won in key congressional races. The developments threaten an already-fragile backdrop for global markets as investors weigh valuations following declines in richly valued tech stocks.

“The political developments in the US may also trigger a slowdown in building up capacity,” Ermotti said. The AI cycle is “definitely going to be a very strong engine of growth, medium to long term. In the short term, it may still be a volatile topic, and that would create potential volatility in financial markets.”

The midterm elections have added a fresh catalyst to the unwinding of the AI trade, which had for weeks faced doubts over whether massive investments in the technology will pay off. Expectations for tighter regulation under a Democratic-controlled Congress are adding to concerns about the growth outlook for chipmakers and data center suppliers, helping drive the steepest decline in US tech stocks since 2020.Ermotti also said inflation remains a key risk that markets are struggling to price. Strong jobs data last week revived expectations for another interest-rate hike from the Federal Reserve.

It is “probably still underestimated how sticky inflation is, and the fact that central banks may need to keep rates higher for longer than expected,” he said.

See also: RBA’s Hunter says AI boom will put near-term pressure on CPI

Ermotti also said he wanted to see more appetite from policymakers in Europe to address concerns over fiscal conditions. Asked whether he was worried about stability of the financial system there following a surge in bond yields in France, Ermotti explained his concern.

“Worried is probably a little bit too far, but I’m concerned that things are not going to be taken seriously enough and fast enough in order to address the risk of contagion, which is probably the most significant one,” he said. “And in that sense, I do hope that the system will come up with urgent measures to contain that potential contagion.”

title: RBA’s Hunter says AI boom will put near-term pressure on CPI
article:
(Nov 9): A senior official at Australia’s central bank said surging investment in areas related to artificial intelligence will further fuel demand in the economy, at a time when policymakers are already aggressively raising interest rates to combat inflation.

In a speech on the potential impact of AI, Reserve Bank assistant governor Sarah Hunter on Monday called it among “the most significant technological developments of our time,” one already beginning to reshape the economy.

“In the near term, the positive shock to aggregate demand set against the economy’s current supply capacity will put some upward pressure on inflation,” she said. “Some liaison contacts are reporting that data centre construction is adding to demand for some already-stretched construction skilled trades.”

Rising construction costs are one channel AI demand is feeding through to the consumer price index, Hunter said during a Q&A after her speech. To a lesser extent, price rises for newer mobile phones and game consoles are also boosting the CPI, she added.

Australia’s construction project pipeline reached a record A$1.4 trillion through September and may end up double the scale of the mining boom, according to Deloitte Access Economics. Both the RBA and government have pointed out the surprising strength of business investment, even as the US-Iran war has pushed energy prices higher and weighed on households.

See also: Nvidia CEO’s affair engulfs AI giant in Chinese spying probe

Still, risks to the AI project pipeline are “balanced,” Hunter said in response to a question, pointing out that potential changes to regulation could crimp some developments.

The RBA has raised interest rates five times this year to 4.85%, an 18-year high, as it struggles to regain control over inflation.

On the upside, once initial bottlenecks are overcome, AI is expected to boost productivity because economies will be able to produce more with the same inputs. That suggests the initial inflationary pressures will dissipate in time, Hunter said in her speech, while acknowledging high uncertainty over the scale of gains.

See also: Australia home sales rise in fledgling sign of property recovery

“Current estimates for the impact of AI on annual productivity growth over the next decade range from over 2% to just 0.1%,” she said.

While Hunter said AI is likely to change the labour market significantly in time, to date it has been fairly muted.

“Contacts in the RBA’s liaison program indicate that AI has not yet impacted most firms’ headcount and is not expected to over the next year,” Hunter said.

“However, there are tentative signs of adjustment, through weaker job ad posting and employment outcomes in more AI-exposed occupations, and stronger growth in areas where the technology has had less of an impact, particularly for younger workers,” she said.

Global financial markets were whipsawed last week after the Democratic Party’s sweep of Congress in the US midterm elections, which stoked fear among investors about tighter regulation of the data center industry.

Hunter said the exposure of financial market participants to the AI investment boom is increasing at a time when investors are demanding very little compensation for taking on risky assets.

“If the returns to AI investment disappoint, some asset prices, including equities and corporate debt, will be exposed to sharp repricing and possibly disorderly adjustments,” she said.

title: Nvidia CEO’s affair engulfs AI giant in Chinese spying probe
article:
(Nov 9): In a 257-word memo to employees, Nvidia Corp chief executive officer Jensen Huang left no doubt that the chip colossus was embroiled in a crisis like none before in its three-decade history.

After months of reports about the CEO’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, Huang admitted on Sunday that he’d had an affair and said the Nvidia board was launching an investigation. Huang had previously said there was nothing inappropriate about his relationship with the woman, who worked for a Singapore-based customer.

“I was unfaithful to my wife,” Huang, 63, said in the memo. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

The stunning admission intensified the controversy surrounding a company at the heart of the artificial intelligence market — a sector that’s already been rocked by concerns about a slowdown in data centre spending. Nvidia makes chips that are crucial to AI computing equipment, and it’s one of the world’s most valuable companies.

Huang himself has been the AI field’s biggest cheerleader, drawing throngs of fans in what’s been called “Jensanity.” Wearing his signature leather jackets, he crisscrosses the globe to help promote the technology’s adoption — a shift he bills as a new industrial revolution. Nvidia also has emerged as a key source of financing for AI infrastructure. He has worked with some of Wall Street’s biggest firms on a US$500 billion effort to help companies rapidly build out their equipment, and he’s funnelled money into bolstering the AI supply chain and fledgling customers.

Though Huang will remain Nvidia CEO pending the results of the investigation, the incident marks a dramatic comedown for an AI evangelist at an already delicate moment.

See also: Australia home sales rise in fledgling sign of property recovery

“It is hard not to read the news over the weekend as negative given it brings the stewardship of one of America’s most important companies, and the architect of the US AI trajectory, under debate, as well as calling judgment into account,” Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon said in a note.

President Donald Trump defended Huang on Sunday, calling him a “fine person” and saying he should remain CEO.

“I have not spoken to him about it,” Trump told reporters. “I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on.”

See also: Thai spyware alerts prompt opposition leaders to demand probe

To investigate the case, the Nvidia board is assembling a committee of independent directors, who will work with outside counsel, according to a statement Sunday. A perpetual futures contract on the Hyperliquid blockchain referencing Nvidia’s share price fell about 2.9% in the wake of the announcement.

The probe follows a series of reports that Nvidia’s leader was targeted by former Megaspeed International executive Alice Huang, who the US government suspects was recruited by a Chinese spy agency. The CEO previously said he had a “normal” business relationship with the woman, who is no longer at Megaspeed.

The board investigation will address reports that the chip magnate “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort,” the company said. “While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board’s inquiry will examine all available information.”

In his memo, Huang said he will support the investigation. “I love our country and our company, and I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security,” he said.

Nvidia’s co-founder — a leader famous for his hands-on and tireless management style — built the maker of graphics cards into arguably the world’s most important technology company. Nvidia’s highly prized accelerator chips are used to develop and run AI models, and Nvidia has branched out into related fields, including computers, networking and software.

Huang also has been a leading voice trying to calm fears about AI technology slipping out of human control. He has dismissed the need for the AI labs to slow down their work to ensure it doesn’t threaten humanity — even at a time when industry leaders such as Dario Amodei and Sam Altman have endorsed such an idea. He’s also argued that new regulations are unnecessary.

The Santa Clara, California-based company has no public succession plan, and there is no obvious heir apparent for Huang. He has repeatedly said he wants to continue in his role for decades and has created an informal organizational structure around him that eschews a conventional hierarchy. Instead, his direct reports are tasked with rapidly implementing his decisions.

Huang has said that this system gives his company the flexibility to react to rapid changes in technology and remain agile. But it’s also created a situation where there’s no replacement ready to step in and take over Huang’s relentless schedule.

The latest revelations “highlight the considerable key man risk that Nvidia faces,” Rasgon said. “Nvidia is not an ordinary company and Jensen is not an ordinary CEO; he IS Nvidia, clearly sets the long term strategy and direction, and (with supposedly 60 direct reports) pulls most of the company’s strings himself.”

Concerns that sensitive information might leak via Nvidia’s contacts with China have fueled calls for investigations and greater scrutiny of Huang and the company, ratcheting pressure in what has already been a difficult geopolitical balancing act. While Nvidia is allowed to ship a limited range of products to China under a licensing program granted by the current Trump administration, Beijing has restricted imports of the chips — an impasse that continues to curb the chipmaker’s sales in the world’s second-largest economy.

Huang has long sought to sell more of Nvidia’s AI processors in China, the largest market for chips. He’s argued that Nvidia and its peers should be allowed to serve the region to keep their products central to the development of AI. Closing off the market will risk turning China into a more powerful, independent force in artificial intelligence, he has said.

Investors have poured money into Nvidia, which reports earnings later this month, betting it will continue to be the main beneficiary of runaway spending on AI infrastructure.

The company reached a record market capitalization of nearly US$5.8 trillion in October. That has slipped below US$5 trillion, however, weighed down by concern about the sustainability of AI infrastructure build-out.

Megaspeed, based in Singapore, has been accused of breaking US export restrictions and smuggling Nvidia chips to China. Huang had told Bloomberg that his contacts with Megaspeed employees were typical of business relationships he has with many Chinese customers and executives.

 Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it. 



 To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust. 



 To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. 



 Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence. 



 Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company, and I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American. 



 My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy.
